title.en: Living Life on Ultimate Terms According to the Dhamma

speaker: Pra Joshua Vajira Panyo
language_note: This talk was written and given in English. There is no Thai translation yet.
_source_note: Written by Pra Joshua Vajira Panyo and given freely. Published exactly as he wrote it, at his request — the wording, spelling and punctuation are his own. Not for sale.

paragraphs.en: Can we live life in ultimate terms, in accordance with the Dhamma?
Living according to the Dhamma does not necessarily mean immediately abandoning ordinary life.
It means learning to live in accordance with reality, rather than being controlled by craving, fear, ego, social pressure, or every thought that arises in the mind.
The Buddha teaches a gradual path.
Sīla — live ethically.
Samādhi — train and steady the mind.
Paññā — develop wisdom and see things as they truly are.
Sati — cultivate mindfulness and awareness.
Non-attachment — enjoy what life offers without making impermanent things the foundation of our happiness.
The Dhamma ultimately points towards Nibbāna: freedom from craving and suffering.
Yet the Buddha also gave practical teachings for people living ordinary household lives.

In the Dīghajāṇusutta, AN 8.54, a householder approaches the Buddha and explains that he enjoys worldly pleasures, lives with his wife and children, uses fine things and handles wealth. He asks the Buddha for teaching that leads to welfare and happiness in this life and future lives.
The Buddha does not simply tell him to abandon everything.
Instead, he teaches four qualities leading to welfare and happiness in this life:
Initiative.
Protection of wealth.
Admirable friendship.
Balanced living.

The Buddha teaches the householder to become capable and diligent in his occupation, protect wealth that has been righteously acquired, associate with good people, and live according to his income and expenditure. (SuttaCentral)
This is important.
The Dhamma is not simply a teaching about escaping ordinary responsibilities.
The Buddha taught people how to live wisely within those responsibilities.

paragraphs.heading: Living Well While Walking the Dhamma

paragraphs.en: A person can earn wealth through right livelihood.
A person can become physically strong.
A person can marry.
A person can raise a family.
A person can enjoy wholesome pleasures.
A person can care for parents, children, partners, friends and the wider community.
These things are not themselves the final problem.
The deeper problem is attachment.
Wealth can become greed.
Strength can become pride.
Beauty can become vanity.
Love can become possessiveness.
Pleasure can become craving.
Success can become conceit.
The Dhamma teaches us to recognise these tendencies within the mind.
So we can build wealth without becoming possessed by wealth.
We can develop a strong body without becoming possessed by appearance.
We can love our family without believing that we can possess them forever.
We can enjoy good food, beautiful places, friendship and comfort while remembering that everything conditioned changes.

The Buddha’s teaching in AN 4.62 is especially relevant here. He describes four kinds of happiness available to a layperson: the happiness of ownership, the happiness of enjoying wealth, the happiness of freedom from debt and the happiness of blamelessness. Yet he places the happiness of blameless conduct above the happiness gained merely through possessions. (SuttaCentral)
This gives us an important perspective.
Wealth can provide comfort.
Blameless conduct provides something deeper.

paragraphs.heading: What Do We Do With Wealth?

paragraphs.en: The Buddha did not teach that wealth has no value.

In AN 5.41, the Buddha explains wholesome uses of wealth acquired through energetic effort and righteous means. Wealth can support oneself, parents, wife and children, workers and others, while also being used for generosity and meritorious deeds. (SuttaCentral)
So the question becomes:
What are we doing with what we have?
When money comes, practise generosity.
When success comes, practise humility.
When responsibility comes, practise diligence.
When criticism comes, practise patience.
When anger arises, observe it rather than becoming it.
When pleasure arises, enjoy it with mindfulness rather than clinging to it.
When something disappears, practise letting go.
When failure comes, learn from it.
When opportunity comes, use it wisely.
Every ordinary experience becomes an opportunity for Dhamma practice.

paragraphs.heading: Building a Good Life and a Good Mind

paragraphs.en: A person can build a good home while building a good mind.
A person can become physically strong while becoming stronger in morality, mindfulness, patience, courage and wisdom.
A person can build a successful career while practising right livelihood.
A person can become financially secure while practising generosity.
A person can have a loving family while contemplating impermanence.
A person can enjoy worldly happiness while understanding that worldly happiness is not the same as Nibbāna.
This is where the Dhamma becomes practical.
Earn honestly.
Live responsibly.
Love generously.
Enjoy mindfully.
Practise diligently.
Let go gradually.
The Buddha’s teaching is a gradual training. Deep understanding does not arise all at once. The path develops through gradual training, gradual practice and gradual progress. (SuttaCentral)
So there is no need to imagine that we must become perfect tomorrow.
We practise today.
Tomorrow we practise again.
We notice craving.
We notice anger.
We notice fear.
We notice pride.
We notice attachment.
We notice the mind creating stories.
Then we learn to see these experiences clearly rather than automatically obeying them.
This is daily Dhamma practice.
The goal is not simply to run away from the world.
The goal is to understand the world clearly.
We use the world without allowing the world to control the mind.
We enjoy what life offers while remembering impermanence.
We build relationships while remembering that every relationship is subject to change.
We build wealth while remembering that wealth cannot accompany us forever.
We strengthen the body while remembering that the body ages.
We enjoy success while remembering that success changes.
We experience pleasure while understanding that pleasure arises and passes away.
And through that understanding, attachment gradually weakens.
Ultimately, the Dhamma points beyond worldly prosperity towards Nibbāna.
The Buddha describes Nibbāna as the highest happiness, while also teaching that the path towards liberation develops through wisdom and the ending of craving. (SuttaCentral)
Therefore, living life on “ultimate terms” does not mean having nothing.
It means not allowing anything impermanent to become the ultimate master of the mind.
We can work.
We can build.
We can love.
We can become strong.
We can raise a family.
We can enjoy life.
We can become successful.
And throughout all of it, we practise the Dhamma.
The question is not simply:
“How much can I get from life?”
The deeper question is:
“While living this life, what is happening inside my mind?”
That is where the real practice begins.
Let the Dhamma be our compass.
Earn honestly.
Live wisely.
Love generously.
Enjoy mindfully.
Practise diligently.
Let go gradually.
Build a good life while building a good mind.
Live fully.
Live wisely.
Live freely.
And walk the path of Dhamma towards the freedom the Buddha called Nibbāna.

bullets: AN 8.54 — Dīghajāṇusutta: guidance for householders on initiative, protecting wealth, good friendship, balanced finances, generosity, ethics and wisdom. (SuttaCentral)
AN 4.62 — Ānaṇyasutta: ownership, enjoyment of wealth, freedom from debt and blamelessness. (SuttaCentral)
AN 5.41 — Ādiyasutta: wholesome uses of legitimately acquired wealth. (SuttaCentral)
MN 70 — Kīṭāgirisutta: the gradual nature of training, practice and progress. (SuttaCentral)
Dhammapada 179–196: Nibbāna and liberation from craving. (SuttaCentral)
